title: Judge rules police had no choice but to shoot man who stabbed his wife
article: The race to save a Calgary woman fatally stabbed by her husband left police no choice but to shoot and kill the suspect when he came at officers with a knife, a fatality inquiry into the case concluded.
Provincial court Judge Judith Shriar made that determination after presiding over an inquiry into the deaths of Sabah Yousif Rizig and Walid Mohamed Maragan on the night of Sept. 4, 2008.
Maragan, 35, attacked Rizig, 33, inside the couple's apartment at 1526 26th Ave. S.W. before calling 911 and informing authorities he had killed her.
One of four officers who arrived at the couple's fifth-floor suite opened fire when Maragan confronted officers with a knife and refused repeated commands to drop the weapon.
With no knowledge whether Rizig was still alive and in need of life-saving assistance, shooting Maragan was the only remaining option after a Taser strike failed to subdue him, Shriar said.

"Because of the known presence of a victim of Mr. Maragan's criminal violence, the police had no choice but to intervene and react in the way they did," she wrote in her report, made public on Wednesday.
The inquiry concluded Rizig was the victim of homicide at Maragan's hands; Maragan's death was classified a non-criminal homicide.

Shriar decided to classify Maragan's death as a homicide after weighing testimony about whether Maragan had intentionally brought about his own death by forcing police into a deadly confrontation - a phenomenon known as "suicide by cop."
Shriar decided against officially classifying Maragan's death as a suicide, saying there was insufficient evidence to stretch the strict definition laid out in legislation.

"The violent, rapid sequence of events render it difficult to draw any reliable conclusions about Mr. Maragan's intention or volition. Given the intense and violent situation, I cannot conclude he was thinking clearly at all, let alone about what he intended for the police to do," she wrote.
Maragan may not have intended for police to shoot him, but Shriar said the issue of suicide by cop warranted consideration.

The judge made three recommendations aimed at training police officers and civilian dispatchers to recognize situations when an armed suspect may try to provoke police into using lethal force - with the caveat they wouldn't have made a difference in Maragan's case.

The judge based her recommendations on the actions of the Calgary Police Service, which developed a training guide for all officers on what's known as "subject-precipitated suicide" in law enforcement.

"The more accurate and timely information can be for the officers on scene, the better their risk assessment and decision-making is going to be," said Insp. Chris Butler, who testified at the inquiry.
Shriar also recommended that police try to find ways of gaining quicker access to social and mental health information about suspects in similar situations.
But legislation governing patient confidentiality prevents that from happening in most circumstances, Butler said.

Members of the Police and Crisis Teams, a specialized unit formed in 2010 that pairs officers with mental health workers, can share that kind of information - but the squad is focused mainly on working with the homeless.

Still, agencies across the country are continuing to wrestle with how to safely and compassionately police people who are mentally ill and pose a risk to themselves or others: a joint conference hosted by the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and the Mental Health Commission of Canada explored the issue last March.
"It's an issue that's foremost in the minds of police and mental health workers," Butler said.
